articles.title: This free creative app is like Internet Archive meets Pinterest
articles.content: Do you remember, as a kid, going through a stack of old magazines and clipping out the sections that you liked? There was an art to it. Whether you were in class or just making some decorations for your wall at home, it was important to find clips that expressed your personality—pictures you thought were interesting or cool or that in some way said something about you. And it was fun to find sentences to put out of context, or even to cut out individual letters to create your own custom messages. But, much as some of us around here may still love them , physical magazines aren’t as omnipresent as they used to be. So how can you recreate that feeling today—and find new ways it can be useful or even just plain enjoyable in your adult life? This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence . Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of awesome tech treasures! Your modern-day collage experience ​Clipart Studio​ is a website that simulates the experience of cutting up magazines to make a collage. ➜ You can page through real vintage magazines, virtually “cut” what you want, and put everything together in any way that suits your fancy. ⌚ You’ll need a mere minute or two to explore the site. Just open the website and get started. In the left panel, you’ll find six random magazines, sourced from the Internet Archive​ . You can browse by topic or click the little die icon to get six more random titles. ✅ Click a magazine, and you can start flipping pages—just the way you remember. When you see something you like, use the virtual knife to cut it out, then place it on your board. Keep doing this as long as you like. Clipart Studio brings old-fashioned magazine collages into the digital age. ☝️ There’s a bit more here, too. You can search for images, sourced from Wikimedia Commons. Or you can drag an image over from your own computer, if you want to make sure your cat (or child, coworker, or whatever the case may be) is featured. With sources from the Internet Archive and Wikimedia Commons, you’ve got plenty of material to work with. The possibilities are practically endless, whether you end up sharing your creation, using it for some social media purpose, or even just enjoying it yourself and not trying to turn it into anything more. (Side note: The site was made by a designer named ​Sami Smith​ , who has a knack for creating fun projects like this. Check out her ​version of Wikipedia running on an imaginary Windows XP desktop​ for another memorable retro-tech adventure. ) Clipart Studio works ​in any web browser​ , on any device. It’s free, and there’s no advertising, either. Your collage is stored in your own local browser, meaning it’s entirely private (though you can optionally share it for a public gallery, if you want). Treat yourself to all sorts of brain-boosting goodies like this with the free Cool Tools newsletter —starting with an instant introduction to an incredible audio app that’ll tune up your days in truly delightful ways.

articles.title: Cisco Gives Engineer Unlimited AI Tokens To Rewrite Legacy Code
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Fortune: Gen Z can't catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco's president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn't buying it -- he's just handed one of the company's biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart "five levels" below him. "I've given him unlimited tokens because he's going to refactor code," Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. "So I'm like, you can go, you can go nuts." The "him" is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or "Paddy," as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel's words, "buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic." That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco's San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco's legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren't thinking that way. So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of rewriting 98% of Cisco's legacy code within 24 months. Now, he's on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will "challenge the system and the status quo," or, as he puts it, be "an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up." "The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we're surrounded by people with a broad range of experience," said Patel. "Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode." "Either of these groups by themselves aren't nearly as potent as when all three work together. It's what creates magic." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

Hello, We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data. We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details). We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m., Central European Time. Report it through Scribd, Inc.'s Help Center. articles.title: The latest Apple Watch update promises better treadmill workout tracking — so I tested it
articles.content: Back when Apple announced watchOS 27 back in June earlier this year, there was one new feature that piqued my interest more than the promise of a smarter version of Siri or a Workout Buddy that now operated more standalone. Apple revealed that it was delivering more accurate distance tracking during walks and treadmill runs. It’s primarily doing that by making improvements to the algorithms that help to calculate the distance covered when you step onto that belt. It's website states that 'improved motion tracking algorithms help measure the distance of your treadmill runs and walks more precisely straight from your wrist.' As a runner that does his fair share of runs on a treadmill (and not just because it’s got cold outside — treadmill running is great for specific pacing and incline drills), I liked the prospect that the best smartwatch ’s indoor activity credentials could now match its very solid outdoor performance — which I tested on the London marathon course’s infamous GPS black spots . So, has Apple actually managed to deliver more accurate distance tracking for indoor runners? I’ve been spending the last couple of months testing the feature across the best Apple Watches — including the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 — to find out. How I tested (Image credit: Getty Images) I began my testing using the beta versions of watchOS 27 running on the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and the Apple Watch Series 11. When watchOS 27 was given a public release, I also strapped on the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the Watch Series 12 to see how Apple’s latest smartwatches fared indoors. I didn’t have my own treadmill (or indeed, have the room to house one), so I relied on the treadmill at my gym. While I did my best to stick to the same treadmill for these test runs, that wasn’t always possible. That did mean I’d be stepping onto treadmills of various conditions and belt wear, which does have an impact on the reliability and accuracy of the treadmill distance tracking feature. With the Apple Watch strapped alone to one wrist, I had a Coros watch on the other paired to the Coros Pod 2. This foot-worn pod is designed to track distance, among other metrics, and was an additional source of data that could offer a more reliable picture of my running distance than the motion sensors that usually do that from the wrist. I used the foot-worn pod as a control device, the same way we use the best heart rate monitors to test the readings from smartwatches. With watches on wrists and the pod on my feet, I captured a range of runs covering different paces and distances. That included short one-mile test runs, steady hour-long runs and interval runs during which I mixed up my pace. I stuck to the same incline for all runs and used Apple’s own Workout app to track the workout. Apple suggests tracking an outdoor run of at least 20 minutes to calibrate the watch and help those algorithms do a better job of understanding your stride length, and in turn, deliver more accurate distance tracking. I did that with each Watch I tested. The results (Image credit: Ljupco Smokovski / Shutterstock) On the early runs in my testing using the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and the Series 11, I found a difference of about 300 metres (0.3km) from the distances the treadmill and Coros Pod 2 reported. If I’m looking at that difference in terms of a longer distance race such as a marathon, that’s quite a small difference. If we’re looking at that difference over a shorter distance race such as a 5km, then it might be the kind of difference that mattered. When I switched to testing with the publicly available version of watchOS 27 with the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the Series 12, there tended to be a difference between the treadmill and watches of roughly 200 metres. Again, that’s a very good performance and a small difference when you’re banking a longer run. Sample run Apple Watch Series 12 distance Coros Pod distance Treadmill distance 1 mile test 1.2 miles 1.01 miles 1 mile…

articles.title: Someone found their lost Bose bud in a field of gravel using ChatGPT, and it's genius
articles.content: Imagine the scene. You're in the park with your family, you're running to catch up with them, and your earbud case falls out of your pocket, scattering your earbuds. You find one but the other has vanished and all you can see is gravel. Who ya gonna call? For Just-a-fungi893 on Reddit , the answer is: ChatGPT. "I spent a solid 10 minutes searching, knowing there's basically no way I'm going to find a tiny white earbud in a sea of white gravel, especially with the sun setting," they explained. "I use ChatGPT for A LOT of stuff, and it suddenly dawned on me to ask it for help instead of pointlessly scanning the area myself." Five minutes later, earbud and owner were reunited, with ChatGPT steering him towards the exact point in the relevant photo. It's not because ChatGPT has magic powers, but because LLMs are really good at spotting tiny things in big pictures: earbuds in gravel, needles in haystacks, indicators of tumors in X-rays. It's all pattern recognition. ChatGPT found my lost earbud from r/ChatGPT It's time to embrace our AI overlords vs no, it isn't As fun as the story is — I'd never have thought of taking a photo and feeding it to a chatbot; it's smart thinking — one of the other comments on the Reddit thread made me laugh: Mindless-Apricot-236 responded that they once lost a screw outdoors, uploaded a picture to ChatGPT and "asked the oracle to help me find it. It said it found it. Showed me the picture... It just modified the original picture and put a random screw on it lol" Other commenters had suggestions that didn't involve AI at all, such as 4-jr1's "how about next time you just open Spotify and listen for the one rock among hundreds that sings out loud" — although that wouldn't work if the headphones weren't on and paired; I have Bose QuietComfort earbuds and they don't turn on until they're in my ears — and SpehlingAirer's "When this kinda thing happens to me I turn on my phone's flashlight and bring it low to the ground pointing almost horizontally. The way the light reflects off the common background (gravel, carpet, grass, etc) and the way it reflects off the glossy plastic are often different enough to help spot it quickly." And of course many of the best earbuds have some variation of Find My, enabling you to locate them from your phone. But it's nice to know that all those years we've been identifying bicycles, stairs and traffic lights in website CAPTCHAs has paid off: computer vision has become really incredible. As to whether it's reliable, I'll just leave this, by AnalogAngeleno, here: "I tried something similar at a used bookstore. Took a photo of the shelve and asked it to help look for books since they were not in any kind of order. Unfortunately it started making up books that were not even there." Still, you'll get different results depending on the type of task and the model you're using — evidently, this one worked well enough, and seems like a good tip to keep in mind for your own earbud emergency.

articles.title: Anduril wants to become a laptop maker — drone and defense giant partners with Qualcomm to build new BlueChip devices, all made in the US
articles.content: Anduril plans to open BlueChip laptop orders in 2027 with Qualcomm BlueChip prototypes source 90% of component procurement costs from American and allied suppliers Anduril expects its laptops to cost 20% more than comparable devices Anduril Industries has revealed plans to enter the laptop market through a partnership with Qualcomm, with plans to begin accepting orders for its BlueChip computers in 2027. The defense technology company, best known for its military drones , intends to reduce reliance on overseas suppliers as it develops the new laptop line. However, its current sourcing figures show that eliminating foreign suppliers remains a future objective rather than an existing achievement. BlueChip begins with American manufacturing The company has developed working prototypes featuring Qualcomm Snapdragon X Series processors, which will power the laptops. Anduril says suppliers in the United States and allied countries account for 90% of the procurement cost of the components used in its prototypes. The company already sources several parts locally, including batteries, computer enclosures and display glass. Its strategy also involves using metals that American industries can extract, refine and process at commercial scale. “Other companies might design their computers in the U.S., Anduril makes them here,” said Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, in a company video. “We’re making parts out of metals that the U.S. knows how to extract, knows how to refine, knows how to process, and knows how to mill at scale at a reasonable price; and that goes for the entire laptop. The same thing goes for the battery technology.” The company says the laptop is designed to withstand demanding environments, with replaceable upper and lower shells that allow users to customize its configuration. These interchangeable panels could accommodate additions such as solar panels, specialised fabric materials and service insignia, according to Anduril’s video. The design also allows flat phased-array antennas to be integrated directly into the laptop’s chassis, potentially supporting specialised applications in demanding operating environments. Anduril estimates that producing a fully American-made laptop could cost 20% more than a comparable device, potentially limiting its appeal to ordinary consumers. Therefore, it appears to be focused on customers with specific security requirements, including government agencies, military organizations, emergency responders, and public safety departments. These buyers may accept higher prices to address concerns about hardware security and supply chain reliability. A domestic supply chain remains difficult Anduril acknowledges that producing complete laptops requires more than processors and selected parts. Circuit boards, displays, batteries, and other essential components remain heavily dependent on foreign suppliers, complicating efforts to eliminate reliance on these suppliers. “BlueChip will take a phased approach, beginning with expanding domestic sourcing and manufacturing, progressing toward eliminating reliance on foreign suppliers, and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain,” the company said in its announcement. The project comes as semiconductor investment grows in the United States, including TSMC’s facilities in Arizona and Samsung’s site in Taylor, Texas. These projects could improve access to locally fabricated chips, but they do not guarantee a domestic source for every part needed to assemble a laptop. Taiwan has also planned support for smaller companies supplying TSMC through industrial parks in the United States. Such initiatives could give BlueChip access to additional suppliers, although their eventual contribution to the laptop’s production remains unclear. Via Tom's Hardware

articles.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI won't slow its math and science paper barrage
articles.content: OpenAI will keep pushing AI’s scientific discoveries, Sam Altman says Some researchers are excited by the ‘fantastic’ breakthroughs But others warn that the pace of change is ‘psychologically taxing’ One of the promises that huge AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have made is that their machine learning models will help to solve some of the oldest problems in math and science. The pace of their discoveries has left many experts struggling to keep up, but OpenAI’s Sam Altman just has just said there’s much more in store — and not everyone is happy about that. Speaking on the Cheeky Pint podcast , Altman outlined his belief that “Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge, and we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery.” That rationale is why OpenAI has published breakthrough after breakthrough in these fields, knocking down some of the oldest and toughest problems that have troubled great thinkers for years. But the way in which the company has set out its results has drawn criticism for often inadequate attributions and questionable verification processes. While Altman acknowledged that, saying on the podcast that “I do have empathy for the method” and saying OpenAI’s quest for mathematical challenges did “get out of control” at times, he suggested that there’s much more to come. Asked if the firm has anymore unpublished breakthroughs in its vaults, he replied “We do. Of course.” That’s led to accusations that, far from giving people “fundamental knowledge,” OpenAI is gatekeeping important discoveries. And there’s another problem: the sheer scale of the new research is swamping academics. For instance, Wired has noted that the company recently “dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub,” leaving the scientific community to pick through the enormous mass of information. And the impact of having the most important work in your life suddenly undercut by a machine is “psychologically taxing for many people,” said Thore Husfeldt of the IT University of Copenhagen. Husfeldt added that there is “a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people.” Obliterating entire fields of research (Image credit: Shutterstock) AI models’ ability to solve thorny problems was keenly demonstrated when it apparently disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH), which argued that the effort needed to solve a problem increases with its complexity. That’s upended countless theories that assumed that ETH was correct and left many experts scrambling to catch up. As Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson told Wired, although AI’s tendency to undermine years-long research can be irksome, “at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.” UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov aptly described the mood among many scientists and mathematicians, saying “It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.” For Husfeldt, meanwhile, the discovery is “fantastic.” He added: “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room. It’s like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.” In the case of the ETH theory, OpenAI’s work has not been peer reviewed or independently verified. But it’s clear that AI research is creating generational changes in many areas — and overturning entire fields of study in an instant, with all the excitement and chaos that comes with that. Jonsson fittingly summed the situation up, saying: “I don’t care if it’s a human-written proof, or it’s written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.”

articles.title: Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio
articles.content: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, speaking at an event in Olympia in June, called out Microsoft last week over a TV ad from a PAC the company has helped fund. (Office of the Governor Photo) Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week. Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer , an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday , saying it was obtained from an unnamed source. In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.” The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief. “What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.” “I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data. The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company. “If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said. He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said. Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said. Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.” He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges. “What we have here is so bloody special,” he said. Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.” The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028. The newsletter said it released just the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported. Mattmiller declined to comment to the Observer, and Ferguson’s office didn’t respond to the publication. GeekWire has contacted Microsoft and the governor’s office for comment. Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records , including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft. Microsoft CEO Satya…

articles.title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
articles.content: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. articles.title: HomeView Software 27.2: Wallpapers, Control Center, and More
articles.content: Apple today released HomeView Software 27.2, which is the software that runs on the upcoming HomeView device set to launch on November 13. The HomeView was announced earlier in October, but the early software release gives us a look at features like wallpapers and reveals a few tidbits we didn't previously know. Wallpapers There are 20 default wallpapers to choose from on HomeView, with a range of colors. Users will also likely be able to set their own photo wallpaper. The HomeView uses faces, but the wallpapers may be shown on the Home Screen . View all 20 photos in the full article → Face Editing Guilherme Rambo shared an image of the HomeView's face editing interface, where users can choose the design they want to use on the HomeView's Lock Screen. Of course I had to virtualize a HomeView 😅 First look at the face editing UI. https://t.co/3t03FVmuP3 — Guilherme Rambo (@_inside) October 30, 2026 Hello Screen At startup, the HomeView will show the familiar "Hello" text. Hello! https://t.co/pXdUR21Gev — Guilherme Rambo (@_inside) October 30, 2026 Control Center A HomeView setup animation shows Control Center on the HomeView. HomeView setup animation found in HomeView Software 27.2 https://t.co/k4gCHNV3bY — Aaron (@aaronp613) October 30, 2026 Light and Dark Mode As with other Apple devices, the HomeView will have Light Mode and Dark Mode options, with the device able to swap between modes automatically based on time of day. Snoopy The HomeView has a bunch of different Snoopy animations if you pick the Snoopy face. Here are the Snoopy videos from the HomeView 🧵 https://t.co/hrRxPlmVSS — Aaron (@aaronp613) October 30, 2026 Launcher Unlike iOS, HomeView doesn't use SpringBoard. It has a new launcher called BreadBoard , and the process for its Control Center UI is called CupBoard. iOS 26 There is a hidden HomeView Software 26 graphic in the update, which adds to evidence that Apple wanted to release the HomeView earlier but had to wait on Siri AI. Apple also appears to have been testing the interface on a sixth-generation iPad mini before launch. HomeView Software contains this image, adding more indiciation it was initially going to ship with HomeView Software 26 last year https://t.co/yV1a1lbJcr — Aaron (@aaronp613) October 30, 2026 The HomeView is priced at $299, and it can be pre-ordered from Apple's website. It will launch alongside the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K on November 13. Related Roundup: Apple HomeView Buyer's Guide: HomeView (Buy Now) Related Forum: HomePod, HomeView, CarPlay – Home & Auto Tech This article, " HomeView Software 27.2: Wallpapers, Control Center, and More " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
articles.content: In an opinion piece for 404 Media, Matthew Gault argues that Apple has entered its "slop era," abandoning its reputation for innovative hardware in favor of recycled ideas and questionable design choices. Here's an excerpt: My ears perked up when I heard Apple's new foldable phones were cracking. I licked my lips when the company announced it's releasing a touch-screen laptop. This was a company that once charged $19 for a polishing cloth, asked $200 for a VESA mount, and sold $700 wheels for the Mac Pro. Now it's borrowing tired ideas from its competitors and launching hardware its previous leaders rejected. The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus is the new CEO -- a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the much reviled Touch Bar and lawsuit inducing butterfly keyboard. With Ternus at the helm, I feel there's a good chance Apple's best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it's declasse. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It's in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to "Think Different" is now releasing hardware that's just like everything else on the market. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD

articles.title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
articles.content: Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget? Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume. The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence. In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults. The operating model in one view Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing. Figure 1: The five-stage operating model, run as a continuous loop Stage 1: Attribute every dollar You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock ): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 , and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys. Setup is four steps: Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export. Tag your IAM principals with…

articles.title: Flesh-eating screwworms spread to third state and are attacking pets
articles.content: For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people's pets. This week, the country's New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date, 74 animal cases have been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June. The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds, before dropping to the ground to develop into adults. Read full article Comments
articles.author: Beth Mole

articles.title: Oh captain, our captain: Ars staff remembers Patrick Stewart
articles.content: Along with the rest of the world, we at Ars are mourning Sir Patrick Stewart —the beloved award-winning actor best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise—who died yesterday at the age of 86. A statement released by Stewart's representatives said: We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace. Through the actor's X account , the family has requested that, in lieu of flowers, memorial contributions be made to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources . articles.title: Apple Alerts Stores to iPhone Duo's Display Cracking Issue
articles.content: In a memo shared with Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers this week, and later obtained by MacRumors , Apple provided technicians with guidance on how to diagnose and address the iPhone Duo's inner display cracking issue. If a customer reports the issue, Apple advised technicians to inspect the iPhone Duo and repair or replace it in accordance with their standard procedures. While the instructions themselves are straightforward, the fact that Apple issued an internal memo suggests the issue is widespread enough to warrant official guidance. Apple's memo said the issue affects a small number of iPhone Duo units, which is consistent with what it said in a public statement on Monday. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," said Apple, in a statement shared with MacRumors . If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement." You can get support on Apple's website or by calling 1-800-APL-CARE in the U.S. and Canada. Apple said most iPhone Duo units are not susceptible to this issue and that impacted units appear to exhibit the defects rather quickly after usage. Apple said there is no iPhone Duo recall, and the company has yet to launch a public-facing repair program on its website for this issue. Almost immediately after the iPhone Duo began arriving to customers a week ago, a handful of early adopters reported that the device's inner display had cracked , resulting in lines appearing down the middle and towards the right side of the screen. The electronics repair website iFixit completed an iPhone Duo teardown and said that the issue is likely related to a defective hinge on affected units. However, Apple has yet to comment on the underlying cause of the issue. articles.title: Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips
articles.content: Madrona Prize honorees with representatives from Madrona at the Allen School Research Showcase. From left: Karan Mehandru, Chris Picardo and Joe Horseman of Madrona; Zhihan Zhang, Madrona Prize winner; Tanush Yadav, first runner-up; Jacob Morrison of Madrona and the Allen School; and Phoebe Riser and Baxter Black of Madrona. (Photo by Kristine White) A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday. Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus. Zhihan Zhang explains his Madrona Prize-winning research on using AI agents to fit AI models onto small chips. (Photo by Kristine White) Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project . It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat. In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds. The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research. The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena , as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project. Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd. Keisuke Kamahori with his VibeSys poster, winner of the People’s Choice award. (Photo by Kristine White) The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups. Its first application, VibeServe , writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project. Tanush Yadav, first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, with his VideoNet poster. (Photo by Kristine White) The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize , Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet , a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields. Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points. Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project. Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi. Henry Wong, second runner-up for the Madrona Prize, with his poster on securing DNA synthesizers. (Photo by Kristine White) The second runner-up , Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic…

articles.title: Apple Says iOS 27.3 Beta Coming Next Week
articles.content: Apple today announced that the first iOS 27.3 developer beta will be released next week and enable some Apple Intelligence features in China . In a press release shared on the Apple Newsroom website in China, Apple said the beta will be released on Wednesday, November 4, but that likely means Tuesday, November 3 in the U.S. due to time zone differences. Apple said iOS 27.3 will then be released to the public in December, but it did not provide a specific date. iOS 27.3 will enable some of the earlier Apple Intelligence features on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer in China, such as Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up, Notification Summaries, Priority Notifications, Visual Intelligence, and Live Translation with AirPods. Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features announced at WWDC 2026 will not be available in China on iOS 27.3, according to Apple. Image Playground will also not be available in China. Apple also said it has partnered with Alibaba to add support for its AI assistant Qwen within Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence. Both the iPhone and Siri language will need to be set to English and Chinese (Simplified). Apple Intelligence features will not be available on the Mac, iPad, or other devices in China until Apple receives the necessary approvals, it said. articles.title: Need To Rethink How AI Infrastructure Is Powered: FuelCell Energy CEO
articles.content: FuelCell Energy President and CEO Jason Few discusses public concerns over higher utility bills, water use and fossil-fuel infrastructure. articles.title: Supersonic airliner in doubt as company shifts to powering AI data centers
articles.content: Boom Supersonic CEO Blake Scholl recently declared “it’s time for a renaissance in energy and in supersonic flight” as the supersonic airliner company unveiled a Colorado factory dedicated to making gas turbines for AI data centers. But Boom may be facing turbulence after early backers for both ventures have questioned the company’s delivery timeline or backed out entirely. One of the company’s first customers, United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, has expressed doubts about Boom’s original plan to deliver the first Overture supersonic airliner in 2029. Kirby’s latest frank assessment came during an interview with the Office Hours: Business Edition podcast that appeared on October 28, 2026. “‘29 is their official timeline,” Kirby told podcast host Monica Langley. “It’s not going to happen in ‘29—it’s going to take longer.” Read full article Comments
articles.author: Jeremy Hsu

articles.title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
articles.content: Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints , you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file. In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses. The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo . How Session endpoints work Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it. You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime : 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports . Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0 . The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl . Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) , each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer , each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access. The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session: https://8090--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/index.html https://8081--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/status It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket. It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting . A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088 , and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it. A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint , which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a…
articles.author: Sundar Raghavan

articles.titleFa: معرفی Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: ساخت اپلیکیشن‌های وب به صورت زنده توسط ایجنت‌های کدنویسی
articles.summaryFa: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore امکان ساخت اپلیکیشن‌های وب را در حین کدنویسی فراهم می‌کند. با استفاده از قابلیت‌های این پلتفرم، کاربران می‌توانند تغییرات را به صورت زنده مشاهده کرده و از هر نوع مدل پایه‌ای و فریم‌ورکی برای ایجنت‌ها استفاده کنند. این روند باعث تسریع در بازبینی و بهبود کاربردهای وب می‌شود.
articles.summaryEn: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore allows for real-time web app development as coding agents build them. Users can observe changes live and choose any foundational model and agent framework, significantly speeding up the review and enhancement of web applications.
insightsFa: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore به توسعه‌دهندگان امکان ساخت اپلیکیشن‌های وب به صورت زنده را می‌دهد.
تغییرات اعمال شده در اپلیکیشن‌ها بلافاصله در مرورگر کاربران نمایش داده می‌شود.

امکان مشاهده زنده تغییرات به توسعه‌دهندگان کمک می‌کند تا سریع‌تر بازخورد بگیرند.
مدیریت پورت‌های معتبر برای هر جلسه، کنترل بهتری بر دسترسی به اپلیکیشن‌ها فراهم می‌کند.

A successful model deployment requires more: GPU drivers, resource allocation, scheduling, networking, and monitoring must all work… Source

articles.summaryEn: Sanstun is a new and advanced implementation of WireGuard, designed based on sans-IO principles and optimized for efficient parallel coordination. Developed in Rust, it is currently attracting significant attention from network security professionals and developers.
insightsFa: Sanstun بر پایه اصول sans-IO بنا شده است.

articles.title: Apple's Flash Storage Suppliers Are Finally 'Getting Their Revenge'
articles.content: The Wall Street Journal 's Rolfe Winkler this week reported that flash storage suppliers once "bullied" by Apple have been "getting their revenge" on the company over the past year due to a severe memory chip shortage, which stems from AI companies building out massive data centers that utilize significant amounts of flash storage and RAM. As the iPhone took off, Apple became the world's largest buyer of flash storage, and naturally that gave the company a lot of leverage in negotiations. The report goes into detail about some of the hardball tactics that were employed by Apple and its former head of procurement, Tony Blevins . "After ordering flash at rock-bottom prices, Apple would refuse delivery at times if flash prices were falling," the report said. "That left suppliers holding piles of unsold chips, including ones custom-made for Apple. Kioxia executives joked they felt like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football—with Lucy always pulling it away." Based in Japan, Kioxia was previously known as the Toshiba Memory Corporation. Apple is also said to have "bullied flash makers into opening their books so it could monitor sales, making sure no one else got a better deal." The report shared another example involving flash storage supplier Sandisk. Apple's other suppliers, such as SK Hynix and Samsung, were not mentioned. "Around the end of 2015, Sandisk refused Apple's requests to send additional supply because it already had customers willing to pay more," the report said. "Blevins threatened a Sandisk salesman with retaliation, saying he would have Sandisk's chief executive, Sanjay Mehrotra, 'crawl on his knees' back to Apple, according to a person familiar with the call." Things changed when the AI era arrived. "Two years ago, Apple bought nearly twice the flash storage of Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Google combined, according to TechInsights estimates," the report said, citing a research firm. "Hyperscalers are now buying double Apple's share." Much of the "revenge" has been passed on to customers, as Apple has raised prices on more than a dozen products this year, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, HomePods, the Apple TV, and more, with the company attributing these increases to the memory chip shortage. Apple's former CEO Tim Cook said price increases were " unavoidable ." Apple is not completely immune, though. Higher prices could result in lower demand, and the report said its profit margins on storage upgrades have been impacted. For example, TechInsights estimated that Apple makes a gross profit of $134 when a customer spends $200 to upgrade an iPhone 18 Pro from 256GB to 512GB of storage, down from $185 when a customer opted for the equivalent upgrade for the iPhone 17 Pro last year. "We've worked with many of our suppliers for decades, and we deeply value their partnership over the years," an Apple spokesperson told The Wall Street Journal . "We look forward to continuing our important work together." On an earnings call this week, SK Hynix forecasted that the memory chip shortage will persist through 2030 , so the pendulum may not swing back in Apple's direction for at least four more years. Eventually, though, it probably will. articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.content: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account. In search of cloud credentials “It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here . Read full article Comments

articles.title: Sam Altman Thinks Your PC Is Wasting Precious RAM
articles.content: "Looks like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wants to own all the computing resources and rent out terminals to the world as a way of propping up his business plan, now that debt-ridden AI companies are teetering on the edge," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. Tom's Hardware reports: In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible." When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build. Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark): "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model. OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Dartmouth's provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job
articles.content: On August 9, 2026, Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell wrote a Washington Post op-ed called "Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem." This week, Schnell discovered the depths of the problem himself as he resigned from the university after an advisory committee found that he failed to disclose significant AI use in an academic paper and in the Washington Post op-ed, even though publishers required such disclosure. Schnell didn't make it especially easy for the committee to investigate his AI use; the report uses the term "insufficient cooperation." He did turn over his Dartmouth laptop, but he did not turn over logs from his personal LLM accounts related to the writings in question. Nor did he agree to meet with the committee. The committee did get access to the Claude enterprise account Schnell had used through Dartmouth, though. This shows him using the LLM as a tool for revising his papers, finding and fixing bugs in code, and editing or generating figures. articles.title: Darkbloom, which allowed Mac users to rent out their GPUs for AI inference, warns of low payouts
articles.content: Declining token prices have prompted Darkbloom, a distributed inference network, to reassess its business plans. Darkbloom , a project from Seattle-based tech biz Eigen Labs, has developed software that allows anyone with a sufficiently capable macOS device to rent their GPU through the Darkbloom network for interference jobs. In return, they get paid. Through this network, 800 or so participants – including as of two days ago this reporter – have been able to collect a few cents to a few dollars per day by having their hardware handle AI model prompts submitted through OpenRouter , an AI model gateway. In theory, someone running one of Apple's recently released Mac minis with an M5 Pro chip and 64 GB of RAM could earn as much as $192 per month handling incoming inference jobs, per the company's estimate. That assumes full 24/7 utilization during this period on a sought-after model like Qwen3.6 35B A3B, which sells for $0.065/M input tokens, $0.75/M output tokens. But not every network participant has fully surrendered their Mac hardware to the network. The median earnings of the 50 people on the leaderboard amount to about $5.26 per day, $159.86 per month, or $1,918.50 per year. So the best case estimate presented by Darkbloom looks plausible. But it may not be sustainable. The price of tokens – the unit of AI work – has declined, reportedly down 54 percent since May . Ramp's AI Token Price Index , which tracks the price of tokens from Anthropic and OpenAI, shows similar slippage. For Anthropic, the price per million tokens went from $2.65 on May 1, 2026 to $0.62 on October 22, 2026, a decline of 77 percent. In a message shared with Darkbloom participants on the company's Slack channel, Kydo, one of the Eigen Labs researchers working on the distributed inference network, celebrated the network's processing of its trillionth token while attempting to moderate expectations about the project's viability. "Earnings have been low," said Kydo. "For most providers, I don't expect that it is going to recover soon." Pointing to the computational prowess of DeekSeek's DeepInfer framework , he explained that structural changes in the inference market have affected the supply of tokens. "Data centers have become cheaper," he said. "Output per NVIDIA cluster is up ~20x this year, and their margins are wide enough to cut prices 90 percent and still profit at 50 percent." The flood of tokens in turn has washed away the price advantage Darkbloom had previously. "The market caught up to our price," Kydo explained. "We could go lower, but then most of you would earn even less nothing." Finally, he said, the inference routing market is changing, with OpenRouter moving away from price-based routing and putting more emphasis on decode speed, quantization, and prefill speed. For network participants with older or less powerful Mac hardware – those without top of the line Max or Ultra Apple Silicon – "inference won't be worth running," he said. Kydo went on to outline how Darkbloom aims to adapt to the commoditized token market. This involves analyzing model demand to steer participants toward more sought-after models, and looking at ways to provide other kinds of compute work, like distributed CI/CD jobs. For Mac hardware, the focus now appears to be on clusters of high-end Mac Studios (now available with up to 512 GB of RAM), using Apple's Remote Direct Memory Access ( RDMA ) over Thunderbolt. The CI/CD work, based on the observation that AI agents now make pull requests faster than CI/CD pipelines can handle them, will require sandboxing — something the biz expects to begin testing soon. And Darkbloom also aims to improve the performance of its network (in terms of time to first token) and to look for other token buyers beyond OpenRouter. "The next stretch will be a fight, and I expect many machines will leave and Slack will get quieter," Kydo concluded. "But those who stay will be first in line when new earning opportunities come along. We are…

articles.title: Over 25% of people lie to get antibiotics—and their lies aren't even good
articles.content: A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don't need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drills down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time. In the two linked studies published Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both. But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn't be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That's despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat. Read full article Comments

articles.title: MIT affiliates named 2026 Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Fellows
articles.content: Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni were recently named to the 2026 cohort of AI2050 Fellows. The honor is announced annually by Schmidt Sciences, Eric and Wendy Schmidt’s philanthropic initiative that aims to accelerate scientific innovation. Conceived and co-chaired by Eric Schmidt and James Manyika, AI2050 is a philanthropic initiative aimed at helping to solve hard problems in artificial intelligence . Within their research, each fellow will contend with the central motivating question of AI2050: “It’s 2050. AI has turned out to be hugely beneficial to society. What happened? What are the most important problems we solved and the opportunities and possibilities we realized to ensure this outcome?” AI2050 Senior Fellow Sendhil Mullainathan is the Peter de Florez Professor at MIT with dual appointments in the departments of Economics and Electrical Engineering and Computer Science who is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. His current research is at the intersection of algorithms and people, with a central focus on launching The Bike Shop@MIT , a new research center that works toward more human-centered AI through scalable bicycles for the mind, and innovative new gears for machine learning algorithms. Mullainathan is the co-founder of ideas42, a nonprofit to apply behavioral science; MIT's Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, which promotes the use of randomized control trials in development; and Dandelion Health , which combines proprietary AI tools with real-world patient data. He's the co-author of "Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much." Among other awards, he is a recipient of the MacArthur “Genius Grant”; has been designated a “Young Global Leader” by the World Economic Forum; was labeled a “Top 100 Thinker” by Foreign Policy Magazine; and was named to the “Smart List: 50 people who will change the world” by Wired Magazine (U.K.). He serves on the board of the MacArthur Foundation, is affiliated with the NBER and BREAD, and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. His AI2050 project focuses on the translation of patterns detectable by AI into testable theories. AI2050 Early Career Fellows Alex Damian is an assistant professor in the Department of Mathematics, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, who is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. His research focuses on the mathematical foundations of deep learning, with an emphasis on optimization dynamics and representation learning. He was previously a research fellow at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He received his PhD in applied and computational mathematics from Princeton University and his BS in mathematics from Duke University. His AI2050 project focuses on effective AI model training. Bailey Flanigan is a Theodore T. Miller (1922) Career Development Assistant Professor at MIT, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the departments of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Political Science, and is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. She received her PhD in computer science from Carnegie Mellon University in 2024. In 2024-25, she was a Harvard Data Science Initiative Fellow, hosted at the Harvard Ash Center for Democratic Innovation. Her research combines tools from across disciplines (including social choice theory, game theory, algorithms, statistics, and survey methods) to advance political methodology and strengthen public participation in democracy. She is specifically interested in sampling algorithms, opinion measurement/preference elicitation, and the design of democratic innovations like deliberative minipublics and participatory budgeting. articles.title: Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone
articles.content: Claude Code users on Anthropic’s $200 plan will no longer face a rolling five-hour usage cap , provided their accounts are verified and they have weekly usage left. Anthropic announced the change Friday as it renamed its two top consumer plans. Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra. They still cost $100 and $200 a month, respectively, and current subscribers don’t need to do anything to switch. Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra. Anthropic’s pricing page also lists monthly Claude Platform API credits: $100 with Max and $200 with Ultra. That adds another consideration for developers who use Claude Code while building applications against the API, with each plan bundling API credits equal to its monthly subscription price. Claude Code creator Boris Cherny highlighted the limit change in his own post . What the five-hour cap meant The five-hour limit capped usage within a rolling window, and a demanding task could burn through that allowance much sooner. Claude Code users could hit it midway through debugging or a large refactor and have to wait for a reset despite having weekly usage left. Verification comes first Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away. The company says the checks help prevent fraud and abuse, and it will email users when the cap is lifted. Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away. According to Anthropic’ , verification happens automatically based on account and payment history. There’s no way to request it or speed it up so some users will just have to be patient. The weekly cap remains Ultra users still have the same weekly allowance, and they could use it up sooner without the five-hour limit forcing them to pause. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max. Your chats with Claude count toward the same weekly limit as your Claude Code sessions, whether you’re on the web, desktop, or mobile. Once you use up that allowance, you can turn on usage credits to keep working at standard API rates, though you’ll pay extra on top of your subscription. If you keep hitting the session limit with weekly usage to spare, avoiding those interruptions could make Ultra worth the extra $100 a month over Max, but if you already run out before the week is over, removing the session cap won’t give you more included usage. OpenAI eases its limits A day earlier, OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux announced higher usage limits for Pro subscribers and Business Premium. OpenAI also dropped a planned cut for existing $200 Pro subscribers after customers objected. In a separate pricing decision, the company abandoned an idea to replace token-based billing with flat per-job fees after developers pushed back. The post Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone appeared first on The New Stack .

articles.title: Nvidia store quietly pulls the RTX 5080 following RTX 5090 removal — street prices climb to 2.2X over MSRP
articles.content: First, it was the GeForce RTX 5090 , and now the GeForce RTX 5080 – two of the best graphics cards have gone dark. After the Blackwell flagship left Nvidia's marketplace, the GeForce RTX 5080 followed suit. Prices for the sub-flagship have exploded to more than 2.2X its original $999 MSRP, and the Blackwell-powered graphics card is slowly going out of stock at various U.S. retailers. As with the recent disappearance of the GeForce RTX 5090 on Nvidia’s marketplace, the listings and filters for the GeForce RTX 5080 have also disappeared. While its absence does not necessarily mean Nvidia has discontinued the graphics card, it does raise questions about its status and future availability. This move is especially fishy because other Blackwell SKUs, such as the GeForce RTX 5070 Ti and GeForce RTX 5070 , remain listed on the marketplace, albeit marked as “Out of Stock.” The continued presence of the GeForce RTX 5070 Ti and GeForce RTX 5070 suggests that Nvidia wants to keep the products visible even when they are not immediately available so that consumers can anticipate restocks. The complete removal of the GeForce RTX 5090 and GeForce RTX 5080 breaks that pattern. It fuels rumors that Nvidia has allegedly stopped production of the GeForce RTX 5090 and possibly the GeForce RTX 5080 too, in favor of a rumored GeForce RTX 5080 24GB. (Image credit: Nvidia) Rumors claim Nvidia allegedly stopped producing the GeForce RTX 5090 to repurpose the valuable GB202 silicon into the chipmaker’s RTX Pro Blackwell lineup, which fetches higher margins. This has a lot of credence, since many agree that Nvidia stopped being a gaming hardware vendor long ago and has transformed into an AI provider. Rather than simply discontinuing the GeForce RTX 5090, Nvidia purportedly intends to introduce the GeForce RTX 5080 24GB as the new flagship gaming graphics card. The thing is, a 24GB variant of the GeForce RTX 5080 would solve one of the biggest consumer gripes with the graphics card: the lack of memory. While a GeForce RTX 5080 24GB would offer the same memory as the GeForce RTX 5090, it simply isn't a direct drop-in replacement. The former has 2X fewer CUDA cores, a substantial performance gap that even a 50% memory increase can't make up for. How much money are you willing to spend during the Black Friday sales? The GeForce RTX 5080 launched in January of last year with an MSRP of $999. Demand quickly outpaced supply, and with the rapid price hikes due to the memory shortage, the market price has more than doubled its original MSRP. As of this moment, the most affordable GeForce RTX 5080 in stock, the PNY GeForce RTX 5080 ARGB Epic-X RGB OC, retails for $2,199.99 , which is 2.2X over the original launch price. While some stock remains, it’s selling out fast, and the remaining units will only get more expensive as availability dwindles. At this rate, the GeForce RTX 5080 is unlikely to be available by Black Friday. If you are set on a GeForce RTX 5080, you may have little choice but to act quickly and buy at today's elevated prices. If the GeForce RTX 5080 24GB is indeed legitimate, the graphics card will almost certainly debut at a substantial premium over the original GeForce RTX 5080. Although Nvidia maintains that the RTX 5090 is still alive, the reality suggests otherwise. We have contacted the company for comment regarding the GeForce RTX 5080’s status.

articles.title: Thousands of 'Ghost Students' Use AI to Steal Millions In Student Loans, DOJ Says
articles.content: The Justice Department has charged five people in a crackdown on "ghost student" fraud, in which scammers allegedly use stolen identities and AI to enroll fake students in colleges, complete coursework, and collect federal student loan funds. Ars Technica reports: In a press release Thursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from "a network associated with Kenyan nationals" after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that "this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya," while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun. [...] At a press conference, McDonald was joined by FBI and Department of Education officials to explain how the scheme works. It starts with bad actors purchasing personally identifiable information (PII) of Americans -- most frequently targeting high school graduates who never attended college and went straight into the workforce. Once they have that sensitive data, they fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) while seeking to enroll in universities and community colleges. If accepted, student aid is distributed first to schools to cover tuition and fees, but any leftover money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters. Dozens of Americans have opened bank accounts to act as money mules for fraudsters, the DOJ said. To keep money flowing, bad actors use AI to fill out applications, complete coursework, and even make it appear that a student is attending virtual sessions. "It looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class," McDonald said at the press conference. "Some even create the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present. The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester." So far, the DOE has "identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens," officials said at the press conference. If all those accounts are ghost students, total losses come close to $130 million, the DOJ said. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
